video_title: Inside Whatnot's Bet on Live Shopping
gist: Whatnot co-founder Grant tells his a16z investor that live commerce is 30-40% of all commerce in China versus single digits in the US, and that Whatnot has crossed $8B in sales in each of the last two years with users averaging 95 minutes a day and over 80% of them buying nothing on a given day. The core argument is that live video is demand-expansionary rather than share-shifting, that the seller base (small businesses and brands, not eBay-style resellers) is structurally different, and that trust infrastructure - 40% of headcount plus an LLM-fed rules engine - is the real moat.

themes.theme: US vs China live-commerce penetration gap

insights.claim: Live commerce accounts for roughly 30-40% of all commerce in China but only single digits in the US, a penetration gap Whatnot's founder treats as the central investable opportunity.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Sizes the headroom for US/EU live-shopping platforms: if penetration converges even partway, category leaders compound for years without needing share gains against each other.
insights.quote: I've heard anywhere about 30 to 40% of all commerce is is live commerce in in China

insights.claim: Grant believes the US-China live commerce gap will close with certainty because live selling is a structurally richer and more efficient way to sell, not a cultural quirk of Asian markets.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: The bull case rests on medium economics rather than consumer taste, which makes it portable across geographies and harder for incumbents to dismiss.

insights.claim: Live commerce is demand-expansionary rather than share-shifting: buyers discover items they did not know they wanted, so the addressable market itself grows rather than migrating from existing e-commerce.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: If true, TAM models pegged to current e-commerce GMV understate the opportunity, and share-based competitive analysis against Amazon or eBay is the wrong lens.
insights.quote: the thing with live is it's it's um demand expansionary because um you go in and discover new things you didn't know that you would be interested in

insights.claim: eBay fell from roughly 15% of the overall market ten years ago to under 1% today while still doing about $80 billion of volume, showing the market outgrew the incumbent rather than the incumbent shrinking.
insights.speaker: host, a16z partner
insights.so_what: Rebuts the 'Etsy/eBay ceiling' bear case on Whatnot and reframes eBay's $80B as a floor for long-tail commerce rather than a cap.
insights.quote: eBay was actually, if you go back something like 10 years, it was like 15% of the overall market. And it's 80 billion of volume still, by the way.

themes.theme: Whatnot GMV scale and take-rate posture

insights.claim: Whatnot did over $8 billion in sales last year and has already done over $8 billion so far this year, implying a sharp acceleration in run-rate GMV.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A hard GMV benchmark for pricing Whatnot against public marketplace comps and for tracking whether live commerce is compounding or plateauing in the West.
insights.quote: if you looked at whatnot last year we did you know over eight billion in sales and um so far this year we've done over eight billion in sales

insights.claim: Whatnot deliberately takes only a small fraction of GMV and is explicitly not raising fees, betting that letting sellers keep the majority compounds platform growth faster than take-rate expansion.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Signals monetization upside is being deliberately deferred; near-term revenue models should assume flat take rate, with fee increases as an unexercised option.
insights.quote: we take a small fraction of that and you know we we and we'd like to we're we want to we're not raising fees or doing any of that

insights.claim: The largest businesses operating on Whatnot are doing upwards of $100 million in revenue with EBITDA margins of 20-40%+, built entirely on the platform.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Evidence the channel supports durable, profitable seller businesses rather than gig-scale side income, which underwrites seller retention and platform stickiness.
insights.quote: the biggest businesses on whatnot are probably doing upwards of hund00 million in in revenue and you know with like very strong ebida margins 20 30 40 plus percent

insights.claim: Whatnot users spend roughly 95 minutes a day on the platform, putting a shopping app on par with social and entertainment platforms for engagement.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Engagement at social-network levels means the platform can eventually monetize attention (ads, subscriptions) on top of transactions, a second revenue line not in current GMV models.
insights.quote: Yeah about 95 minutes.

insights.claim: More than 80% of Whatnot users buy nothing on a given day and are on the platform purely to watch and talk, meaning the product is consumed as entertainment first and commerce second.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Standard e-commerce conversion metrics badly misprice the platform; the right KPI set is closer to a media company's than a retailer's.
insights.quote: you know greater than 80% of people don't purchase on a given day. They're just there watching, having fun.

insights.claim: A live storefront costs a seller $0 to set up with an unbounded global audience, versus millions in rent for a Fifth Avenue shop restricted to whoever walks by during business hours.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Zero marginal cost of supply is the flywheel input: cheap seller acquisition drives selection, which drives demand, and it prices pressure onto physical specialty retail.
insights.quote: you can set up for $0 and you can have an entirely global audience that is, you know, unbounded

insights.claim: Whatnot's seller base is structurally different from eBay's early reseller cohort - it skews to small businesses and increasingly brands that typically have brick-and-mortar shops or Shopify stores and would never list on eBay.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Undercuts the comp-to-eBay valuation anchor and implies Whatnot is competing for merchant mindshare against Shopify and physical retail, not auction sites.

insights.claim: The last 20-30 years of e-commerce achieved efficiency by obscuring who the seller is and preventing merchants from building brands, and Whatnot's bet is that reversing that trade-off is what unlocks repeat purchase.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Frames seller identity as the differentiator against Amazon-style commoditized marketplaces and predicts merchant migration toward channels that let them own the customer.
insights.quote: if you're on whatnot, you're going to have your store, you're going to have your brand, you're going to have your customers, they're going to come back to you

insights.claim: Live's volume throughput lets sellers accept deeper discounts, making Whatnot a de facto off-price channel resembling TJ Maxx for apparel and DSW for sneakers with old-season inventory at aggressive pricing.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Positions Whatnot as a liquidation and inventory-clearing channel, putting it in competition with off-price retail and giving brands a margin-managed way to move dead stock.

insights.claim: Whatnot now sells across 100+ categories and women's fashion has overtaken collectibles to become its single largest category.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Proves the format generalizes past the collectibles niche that bears used to cap the company with, and puts it into the largest category in commerce.
insights.quote: women's fashions woman is now our biggest category

insights.claim: Golf on Whatnot is growing hundreds of percent year-over-year with golf shops selling live, an example of niche specialty retail migrating wholesale onto the platform.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A leading indicator to watch: category-level triple-digit growth shows how fast a vertical can flip once a critical mass of specialty merchants arrives.
insights.quote: golf on whatnot is having a huge surge, you know, that's growing hundreds of percent year-over-year

insights.claim: Grant's category-selection heuristic is that anything someone would build a retail shop around - anything you would find in a shopping mall - should work on live commerce.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A screen for where live commerce expands next and which specialty retailers face disintermediation risk.
insights.quote: I think anything that someone would build a retail shop around would work on whatnot

insights.claim: Cars and liquor, beer and wine are named as explicit future categories for Whatnot, alongside additional country launches.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Both are high-AOV, heavily regulated categories - watch for licensing and compliance build-out as the tell that these launches are real.
insights.quote: I want to do cars on whatnot because you should be able to buy a car on whatnot

insights.claim: Live video overcomes the trust barrier in categories that never worked online, exemplified by a San Diego seafood distributor who cold-messaged Whatnot on LinkedIn, went live the following week and sold $3,000-$4,000 of fresh fish in a pilot.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder and host, a16z partner
insights.so_what: Shows the format can unlock previously untradeable perishable categories and give local suppliers national distribution - a new demand channel for food supply chains.
insights.quote: video just really enhances the trust

insights.claim: Collectibles have moved from niche to mainstream pop culture over the past six years, with trading cards functioning as a new asset class where one-of-one cards trade for millions the way fine art once did.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Supports continued growth in the alternative-collectibles complex - graders, marketplaces, and authentication businesses ride the same trend.
insights.quote: a lot of the new art that people are collecting is now like trading cards with that are going for millions of dollars

themes.theme: Trust and safety as the real moat

insights.claim: About 40% of Whatnot's employees work in trust and safety, an allocation the founder frames as running the police force and legal system for a user base the size of two New York Cities.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cost structure of live marketplaces - a barrier to entry for challengers, but also an ongoing opex drag to model into margins.
insights.quote: trust and safety particular on whatnot is about 40% of employees

insights.claim: Whatnot runs a rules engine that ingests billions of data points in under one second, using LLMs to detect live-stream harassment and automatically warn, suspend or ban sellers based on shipping delays, refund rates and seller history.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete production use case for LLMs in real-time moderation at commerce scale - the kind of workload that drives sustained inference demand.
insights.quote: takes in billions of data points at this point in sub 1 second to be able to take down or find any range of bad behavior on the platform

insights.claim: Whatnot explicitly refuses to give sellers AI avatar tools because human connection is the reason buyers return, and any seller who automates away the human presence loses their audience.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A live counterexample to the assumption that AI presenters will take over commerce content - relevant to anyone underwriting AI-avatar or synthetic-influencer startups.
insights.quote: Anyone who's good is not um trying to rip out the human experience.

insights.claim: Whatnot's AI strategy is to first deploy models internally for efficiency - item listing, inferring live-stream metadata for discovery, seller analytics - and then expose those same capabilities to sellers.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A repeatable pattern for AI productization at marketplaces: internal tooling as the proving ground before it becomes a seller-facing feature or SKU.

insights.claim: Grant argues that knowing little about the live-shopping market was a 1000% advantage, because market-first founders build iterations on what exists while user-first founders build the new thing.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: A diligence heuristic that cuts against domain-expertise screens: consumer breakouts often come from founders optimizing for user value rather than market maps.
insights.quote: they don't care about the market at all. They care about whether they're going to enjoy the thing. It provides value.

insights.claim: The live-selling insight came from watching Funko Pop marketplace customers hack social media to sell via live video with broken transactions, shipping, payments and discovery - Whatnot built the integrated version of a behavior users had already invented.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: The classic signal pattern worth screening for: users jury-rigging an unsuited platform is the highest-quality evidence of latent demand.
insights.quote: we saw our customers hacking social media in interesting ways

insights.claim: Whatnot now operates in about 10 countries - US, Canada, five in Europe, plus Japan and Australia - and the counterintuitive finding is that the format and seller dynamics work near-identically across all of them.
insights.speaker: Grant, Whatnot co-founder
insights.so_what: Geographic replicability without localization rework is the strongest argument for aggressive international expansion and for a higher terminal multiple.
insights.quote: we've just seen it work in the same way across all of those countries
